1.pericope_label: He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy... The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it

schools.summary: Delitzsch grants that the man of reproofs makes the immediate impression of a censurer on a reader of this book, but sets that aside on grammar, since the noun after man elsewhere in Proverbs names what proceeds from the subject rather than what he does to others; alone among the voices he renders the ruinous figure of the fourth verse a man of taxes rather than a taker of bribes, making the second line describe exaction and not corruption; he rejects two scholars who translate the fifth verse as circumventing a neighbour with flatteries, since the preposition carries no hostile intention and the harm follows whether the flatterer means it or not; and he defines the knowledge of the seventh verse as recognition of what is due to men of low estate simply as men. Ellicott makes the hardened neck a refusal to bear the easy yoke and presses the closing words of the first verse, the man being not destroyed merely but shattered like a potter's vessel that cannot be mended; he glosses the gifts of the fourth verse as taken to pervert justice, sends the reader to the parable of the prodigal for the third, and gives the last verse a face, the wicked man caring as little for his poorer neighbour as Dives did for the beggar at his own door.

Gill offers both senses of the man of reproofs — one who censures others while doing the same things, needing an impudent face and a brow of brass, or, as he prefers, one often reproved — and records that the accents in some copies allow a different division at the sixth verse, an evil snare rather than an evil man. On the seventh he enters a caution none of the others make: the poor man's person is not to be favoured in judgment any more than the rich man's, an affectation of mercy being as much a perversion as partiality the other way, so that what is considered is the cause and not the man.

Clarke supplies a national instance at the fourth verse, that the selling of justice was notorious in England before the great charter, whose article promising that justice would be sold to none was framed against it, and that he has met with cases where a man nearly ruined himself in presents to the king, the queen and their favourites to win his suit; at the third he renders the clause that he who feeds harlots utterly destroys his substance and asks whether there has ever been a single case to the contrary. Wesley glosses the gifts of the fourth verse plainly as bribes.

Henry lists the reprovers of the first verse — parents and friends, magistrates and ministers, providence and conscience — and observes that some will not give the reproof a hearing while others hear it and go on in the sin; treats the proverb on rulers as a repetition, the people both having cause to rejoice or mourn and actually doing so; makes an etymological point of the son who loves wisdom, that such a man is properly a philosopher, that word meaning a lover of wisdom and religion being the best philosophy; reads the flatterer as commending good that is absent or misrepresented, with an ill design, whence his rule that it is wisdom to suspect flatterers; and makes the sin of the sixth verse its own punishment, the transgressor held in the cords of his own iniquity.

debates.question: Who is the man of reproofs in the first verse?

positions.view: Both readings stand: either one who censures others while doing the same things, or — the better sense — one often reproved by others.
One often corrected: the censurer is the first impression, but the construction elsewhere in this book decides against it.
One often reproved, and by every kind of reprover — parents, friends, magistrates, ministers, providence and conscience alike.
Not raised; the interest is in the hardened neck that will not bear the easy yoke, and in a ruin that shatters past mending.

debates.question: What is it that overthrows a land in the fourth verse?

positions.view: Bribery, the taking of gifts to pervert justice.
Bribery, and notoriously so in living memory: justice was sold in England before the great charter forbade it.
Taxation rather than corruption: the ruinous figure is a man of taxes, and the second line describes exaction.

outliers.note: Reads the proverb on ruinous rulers against English legal history, citing the charter clause that justice would be sold to none and records of suitors nearly ruining themselves in presents to the king and queen.
Denies that the flatterer need intend any harm at all: the preposition carries no hostile tendency, and the web woven before a neighbour's eyes becomes a net simply by his being caught in it.

themes: He, that being often reproved hardeneth his neck, shall suddenly be destroyed, and that without remedy.
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
Whoso loveth wisdom rejoiceth his father: but he that keepeth company with harlots spendeth his substance.
The king by judgment establisheth the land: but he that receiveth gifts overthroweth it.
A man that flattereth his neighbour spreadeth a net for his feet.
In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare: but the righteous doth sing and rejoice.
The righteous considereth the cause of the poor: but the wicked regardeth not to know it.

8.pericope_label: Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath... The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the verb of the eighth verse to mean blowing rather than ensnaring, so that the inhabitants of a city are stirred until they burn; reports that Jerome and Luther made the wise man the subject throughout the ninth verse, though his own rendering gives the raging and laughing to the fool; declines the nearest translation at the tenth, making the men of blood the subject of both clauses rather than have the upright seek the guiltless man's life; argues that the noun of the eleventh is not spirit in the sense of what a man has in mind but passionate emotion, since the contrasting verb means not to restrain but to hush up; and reads the second man of the thirteenth as the usurer. Ellicott renders the eighth verse to fan the passions, with the wise allaying anger by gentle counsels; sets out both readings of the ninth without choosing; turns the second clause of the tenth into active charity, the just caring for the life of the perfect man; prefers the oppressor at the thirteenth, and finds in the lightening of both men's eyes a word to each.

Gill reports the Greek and Syriac reading of the eighth verse, that the scornful burn a city rather than ensnare it; notes that the Targum and three ancient versions read wrath rather than mind at the eleventh; and sees Solomon in the last verse of the group with the Messiah behind him.

Clarke quotes Coverdale's old version at the ninth verse, which keeps the reading in which the wise man gets no rest whether he deals with the fool gently or roughly; turns the eleventh into counsel of another sort, that a man should never deliver his whole mind while other opinions are still to come, since if he speaks again he must go over old ground; supplies the sharpest note in the chapter at the twelfth, that wherever a system of espionage prevails a system of falsity is established with it and that he has seen the same spy take pay from both parties and deceive both; and surveys the versions at the thirteenth, calling the second word hard to fix. Wesley glosses the second clause of the tenth verse in two words, to preserve it.

Henry draws the fullest portrait of the scornful men who endanger a city, every clause turning on the scorn itself — they act precipitately because they scorn to deliberate, illegally because they scorn to be hampered by laws, break faith because they scorn to be bound by their word, and provoke the people because they scorn to please them. He states the upshot of contending with a fool, that with a wise man one may hope to be understood but with a fool there is no end of it; notes that bloody men especially grudge upright magistrates who would restrain them; describes the fool as the man who has in his mouth whatever is in his thoughts; judges the ruler who listens to lies as severely as the liar, the receiver being as bad as the thief; and states what faithful judgment of the poor excludes as well as requires, that they are not to be countenanced in an unjust cause for their poverty's sake, but neither may their poverty prejudice a just one.

debates.question: Who rages and laughs in the ninth verse?

positions.view: The fool, who is violent or supercilious by turns and will not listen quietly to argument.
The wise man, on the old reading Coverdale preserved: he gets no rest whether he deals with the fool gently or roughly.
Either; the wording will bear both and the point stands under each.
Not the question; what matters is that with a fool there is no end of the contention.

debates.question: Who is the poor man's opposite in the thirteenth verse?

positions.view: Hard to fix: the versions give the man of little wealth, the usurer, the creditor, the lender, the rich, the oppressors — and the sense of the parallel proverb must settle it.
The usurer.
The oppressor, who is warned by the same light that comforts the poor man.
Not identified; the meeting itself shows providence serving its designs by persons of contrary conditions.

outliers.note: Turns the ruler who listens to lies into a note on espionage, holding that wherever such a system prevails a system of falsity is established with it, since a man who will be a spy will cut his king's or his father's throat — and reporting that he has seen the same spy paid by both parties and deceiving both.

Refuses the nearest translation of the tenth verse, that the upright seek the guiltless man's life, on the ground that the contrast forbids it, and makes the men of blood the subject of both clauses instead.

themes: Scornful men bring a city into a snare: but wise men turn away wrath.
If a wise man contendeth with a foolish man, whether he rage or laugh, there is no rest.
The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.
A fool uttereth all his mind: but a wise man keepeth it in till afterwards.
If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.
The poor and the deceitful man meet together: the Lord lighteneth both their eyes.
The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever.

15.pericope_label: The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame... Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him

schools.summary: Ellicott gives the neglected child of the fifteenth verse a figure, left to wander unchecked like the wild ass, and lays the shame on the mother whose indulgence ruined him; adds that the righteous will see the fall of the wicked with joy, having long expected it; renders the eighteenth verse that the people run wild for want of revelation, God teaching none by his Spirit to instruct others; is blunt at the nineteenth that a slave must be corrected by sterner means, since only fear of punishment moves him, and reads the second clause as a refusal to answer a call rather than an inability to understand it, setting the willing obedience of a son against the grudging obedience of a slave. Delitzsch judges the sixteenth verse in the main a trivial saying and reports the Swabian word for that kind of truism; renders the eighteenth that without revelation a people becomes ungovernable, and marks the verse as important for judging how the wisdom writings stand to prophecy; and puts the last verse of the group as the hasty man blocking his own path to a wisdom that still stands open to the dull, the one being finished while of the other something may yet be made.

Gill turns the rod of the fifteenth verse toward God's own children, who grow wiser under chastisement, and calls that man wise who hearkens to the rod and to him who appointed it; takes the vision of the eighteenth for prophecy in the sense of the public ministry of the word, so that the verse describes a want of men to administer it, instancing the days of Eli and Asa; and keeps the proverb on servants to one kind, since a well-disposed servant needs only a word — bid to go, he goes — and it is the surly who must have blows.

Clarke draws a doctrine of national judgment from the sixteenth verse, that wicked nations and families are cut off and rooted out, and that were it not so righteousness would in time be banished from the earth, which he thinks accounts for many instances in which whole families fail; and at the eighteenth quotes an old English Bible which followed the Vulgate in reading that the people shall be scattered, stating the rule that where divine revelation and faithful preaching are neither reverenced nor attended, the ruin of that land is not far off. Wesley takes the vision for prophecy and public preaching, and makes the servant of the nineteenth a servant in the temper of his mind and not only in condition.

Henry insists that rod and reproof belong together in a fixed order — if a reproof will serve without the rod it is well, but the rod must never be used without a grave reproof beside it — and backs the promise with a Latin tag, that vexation sharpens the intellect. He describes the emboldening of sin rather than its judgment, transgression growing more impudent when many keep it in countenance, as in the old world where men degenerated as soon as they began to multiply; describes the satisfaction of a well-taught child as one none know but those who have it; declines to choose among the senses of the eighteenth verse, since the word has many significations and any will apply, the people being made naked and stripped of their ornaments or their armour; and has more hope of making a scholar of a man dull and slow in his studies than of one with a mercurial genius who cannot fix.

debates.question: What happens to a people without vision?

positions.view: They become ungovernable, the verse bearing on how the wisdom writings stand to prophecy.
They run wild, God teaching none by his Spirit so that others may be instructed.
They are scattered, on the Vulgate's reading preserved in an old English Bible; and where revelation and faithful preaching are neither reverenced nor attended, the land's ruin is not far off.
The word has many significations and any will apply: the people are made naked, stripped of their ornaments and exposed to shame, or of their armour and exposed to danger.
They perish for want of the public ministry of the word, as in the days of Eli and of Asa.

debates.question: Can a servant be reached by words at all?

positions.view: No: a slave must be corrected by sterner means, since only fear of punishment moves him, and his silence is refusal rather than incomprehension.
Only one kind of servant is in view: a well-disposed one needs a word only, and it is the surly and untractable who must have blows.
The man is a servant in the temper of his mind and not merely in his condition, which is why words fail with him.
Not addressed at this verse; the discipline in view is that of the house and of the child.

outliers.note: Dismisses the proverb on multiplying wickedness as in the main a truism, and reaches for the Swabian dialect word for that kind of self-evident saying.
Quotes his own fourteenth-century English Bible at the verse on vision, which followed the Vulgate in reading that when prophecy fails the people shall be scattered.

themes: The rod and reproof give wisdom: but a child left to himself bringeth his mother to shame.
When the wicked are multiplied, transgression increaseth: but the righteous shall see their fall.
Correct thy son, and he shall give thee rest; yea, he shall give delight unto thy soul.
Where there is no vision, the people perish: but he that keepeth the law, happy is he.
A servant will not be corrected by words: for though he understand he will not answer.
Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him.

21.pericope_label: He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length... An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports how far the obscurity of the twenty-first verse reaches, the Greek translators having no answer to its last word and the Talmud resorting to an alphabet cipher to reach a meaning; describes the mechanism of pride, the haughty man obscuring the very honour he has by boasting of it immeasurably and aspiring after more; reports a rival construction of the twenty-fourth verse which would make its first line the predicate of the second, and does not adopt it; and answers a scholar's remark that a warning against the fear of man sounds strange in an eastern book by pointing to a prophet who gives the same warning. Ellicott allows that confidential slaves sometimes did rise to be their master's heirs, but thinks the warning here is against over-indulgence until a servant forgets his position; asks what an angry man will not say and do once anger has overcome him; corrects the second clause of the twenty-third verse, which he would render that the lowly in spirit lay hold upon honour rather than that honour upholds them; identifies the cursing of the twenty-fourth as the judge's adjuration that anyone with knowledge of a theft must inform, so that silence makes a man an accomplice; and holds the ruler's approval of little value, since God decides what each man is really worth.

Gill takes the case of pride back to Adam, who by affecting to be as God lost God's image and was brought to beggary and rags; and distinguishes the fear of the twenty-fifth verse from the fear of God, which leads to no snare, this being a servile fear with torment in it.

Clarke says the pampered servant forgets his obligations and assumes the rights of children; takes the hatred of his own soul in the twenty-fourth verse for his life, which the outraged law may seize at any time; turns the fear of man directly on the reader, that where the mighty have been slain he will fall too unless he calls on the Strong for strength, and must not be ashamed of Christ or his people or his cross; supposes the ruler's favour sought to escape the punishment the law has determined, and observes that a pardon so obtained does not take away guilt in God's sight; and closes on a textual curiosity, the line some copies of the Latin version add about the son who keeps the word not falling into perdition. Wesley expects the indulged servant to grow insolent.

Henry calls the indulgence of a servant imprudent, since he is thereby spoiled for any other place, and holds that servants must endure hardness; has the angry man blowing the coals until he forces even those who would live quietly to fall out with him, and calls undue anger a sin causing many others; supplies three instances of the fear of man at once — Abraham denying his wife, Peter his Master, and many a man his God and religion; notes that Solomon was himself a ruler and knew with what sedulity men applied to him, calling it the way of the world to make interest with great men and expect much from the smiles of second causes; and finds in the last verse not only the natural contrariety of virtue and vice, like light and darkness or fire and water, but the old enmity between the two seeds, while insisting that the sanctified bear good will to all souls and hate only the practices of the impious.

debates.question: What does it mean that the pampered servant becomes a son at the last?

positions.view: The word itself is obscure — the Greek had no answer to it, and the Talmud reached a meaning only by an alphabet cipher.
Confidential slaves sometimes did become heirs, but the warning here is against spoiling one until he forgets his place, as petted servants grow dictatorial.
He is spoiled for any other place, the indulgence being imprudent in the master rather than dangerous to the household.
He assumes the rights and privileges of children, forgets his obligations, and grows insolent.

debates.question: Is the ruler's favour worth seeking?

positions.view: No: it is commonly sought to escape a punishment the law has determined, and a pardon so obtained does not take away guilt in God's sight.
No: his approval is of little value, since it is God who decides what each man is really worth.
It is the way of the world, and Solomon knew it as a ruler himself — but it is expecting much from the smiles of second causes.
The second line may be read of the judgment passed upon a man rather than the judgment he receives.
What is decided by God is the outcome of a man's cause and of all his endeavours.

outliers.note: Ends the chapter on a textual curiosity, that some copies of the Latin version add a line about the son who keeps the word not falling into perdition — a line that stood in the manuscript behind his own old English Bible.
Illustrates the fear of man with three failures at once: Abraham denying his wife, Peter denying his Master, and many a man denying his God and his religion.

themes: He that delicately bringeth up his servant from a child shall have him become his son at the length.
An angry man stirreth up strife, and a furious man aboundeth in transgression.
A man’s pride shall bring him low: but honour shall uphold the humble in spirit.
Whoso is partner with a thief hateth his own soul: he heareth cursing, and bewrayeth it not.
The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the Lord shall be safe.
Many seek the ruler’s favour; but every man’s judgment cometh from the Lord.
An unjust man is an abomination to the just: and he that is upright in the way is abomination to the wicked.
